spec.title: Learning How to Learn
spec.project: Build a one-week learning plan, collect delayed evidence, and revise the plan from what happened.
constraints: Treat confidence as a prediction to check, not proof.
Use practice that produces inspectable evidence.

outcomes.title: Tell the difference between feeling and performing
outcomes.description: A feeling of knowing is a prediction. Check it against what you can actually do later.

outcomes.title: Build knowledge you can actually get back
outcomes.description: Use retrieval, well-chosen cues, spacing, and interleaving on a target you care about.

outcomes.title: Read effort as data, not a verdict
outcomes.description: Struggle tells you where to aim next. Ease while rereading tells you almost nothing.

outcomes.title: Lean on help until you don’t need it
outcomes.description: Learn from worked examples, explanations, and feedback, then strip the supports away and attempt it cold.

outcomes.title: Turn your records into a better routine
outcomes.description: Plan it, look at what actually happened, and change one specific thing for next time.

kcs.name: Records beat feelings
kcs.description: What you managed to do is stronger evidence than how the studying felt.

kcs.name: Calibration: guess, then check
kcs.description: Predict how well you will do, then hold that prediction up against what actually happens.

kcs.name: Does it survive, and does it travel?
kcs.description: Check what you still recall days later, and whether you can use it somewhere new.

kcs.name: Try first, hint second
kcs.description: Attempt recall before you look. Then use a cue that points at the target without handing it over.

kcs.name: Spread it out, mix it up
kcs.description: Return to material across days, and mix related problem types when picking the right method is the hard part.

kcs.name: Effort is a signal, not a score
kcs.description: A hard recall attempt shows you what needs work. It is not itself a grade of your learning.

kcs.name: Familiarity is a liar
kcs.description: Material can feel perfectly familiar after rereading and still be gone when you actually need it.

kcs.name: Chunk by meaning, not by proximity
kcs.description: Group pieces by a relationship you can explain and use, not because they happen to sit next to each other.

kcs.name: Borrow the scaffolding, then take it down
kcs.description: Use a worked example or prompt as temporary support, then remove parts of it before you work alone.

kcs.name: Say why, not just what
kcs.description: Explain why a step follows from a principle, not merely what the step is.

kcs.name: Name the error, then test the fix
kcs.description: Classify what went wrong, correct it, and choose a next attempt that can actually check the correction.

kcs.name: Decide before you start
kcs.description: Pick a target, a practice condition, and a later check, before the session begins.

kcs.name: Reflect on the record, not the vibe
kcs.description: Use your predictions, attempts, and results to name one specific thing to change.

kcs.name: Change something you can test
kcs.description: Adjust the next attempt in response to evidence, instead of repeating a routine you never checked.

content.positive: After studying five vocabulary terms, write down ‘I will get 4 of 5 tomorrow’, hide the list, then tomorrow record your real score and use one term in a fresh sentence.
content.negative: Read the list until all five terms look familiar, then write down ‘felt easy.’
content.explanation: The first gives you a prediction, a delayed check, and a use in a new context. The second cannot tell familiarity apart from actual retention.

content.positive: Monday: recall the steps of a ratio problem from memory. Wednesday: mix ratio and percentage problems, reaching for the hint ‘part-to-whole?’ only once an attempt stalls.
content.negative: Do every ratio problem in one sitting, rereading the formula whenever the answer does not arrive instantly.
content.explanation: The first makes retrieval, a limited cue, a later return, and choosing the method all visible.

content.positive: A learner splits a proof into claim, reason, and consequence, then explains the links from memory even though it takes a pause.
content.negative: A learner highlights the proof twice and treats the smooth second read as proof they could rebuild it.
content.explanation: The pause is information worth chasing. Meaningful groups plus an explanation give you something to test later.

content.positive: First label why each step in a worked solution applies. Then solve a similar problem with the reasons stripped out, and sort any mistake into selection, execution, or explanation.
content.negative: Copy the worked solution, check only the final number, and run the same problem again unchanged.
content.explanation: Support fades, and feedback changes the next attempt instead of stopping at the correction.

content.positive: Plan two 10-minute retrieval attempts and a Friday check. When the record shows solid definitions but shaky examples, add changed-context example practice next week.
content.negative: Plan to ‘study harder’ and keep the same routine after a result you never wrote down.
content.explanation: A plan names its evidence, reflection reads a record, and adaptation is a change you can test.

misconceptions.name: If I feel sure, I know it
misconceptions.diagnostic_probe: You are 95% sure right after reading it. What would actually show, tomorrow, whether that confidence was earned?
misconceptions.correction: Record the prediction, the delayed recall result, and one use in a new context. Confidence on its own is not evidence.

misconceptions.name: Rereading counts as practice
misconceptions.diagnostic_probe: Which one makes you produce the answer before you see it: rereading a definition, or covering it and recalling it?
misconceptions.correction: Retrieval means attempting before the answer appears. A cue can come after the attempt, but it cannot replace it.

misconceptions.name: If it feels hard, I am failing
misconceptions.diagnostic_probe: Does a difficult recall attempt prove you learned nothing, or does it show you exactly what to work on next?
misconceptions.correction: Effort is a signal to check against your records. Structure you can explain makes later retrieval more reliable.

misconceptions.name: Watching it done means I can do it
misconceptions.diagnostic_probe: After a worked example, what would show you can pick and justify a step without its labels there?
misconceptions.correction: Fade the prompts, attempt a related case, and use feedback to classify an error and then test the correction.

misconceptions.name: Reflection means writing how it went
misconceptions.diagnostic_probe: Which recorded result would actually justify changing tomorrow’s practice?
misconceptions.correction: Use predictions, attempts, and outcomes to pick one observable change, then check it later.

content.title: Turn a hunch into something testable
content.body: Name one target, call your shot on how well you will do later, and book a delayed recall plus one use in a new context. Keep the prediction sitting right next to the result.

content.prompt: You are learning three new terms today and checking them tomorrow. Write the evidence plan.
content.solution: A plan that holds up predicts a score, hides the terms for a delayed recall, and puts one term into a fresh sentence tomorrow.

content.title: Attempt first, peek second
content.body: Cover the answer and take a real swing at it. Only then reveal a small cue. Put the next attempt on a later day, and mix in one neighbouring problem type.

content.prompt: Take a formula you are learning and turn it into a two-session retrieval plan with exactly one useful cue.
content.solution: Attempt the formula before you see it. Use a cue such as the quantity relationship only after that attempt, then come back later with a related formula problem.

content.title: Read the signal inside the struggle
content.body: When recall gets effortful, mark exactly which link went missing, regroup the material by a relationship you can explain, and come back later. Do not let ease deliver the verdict.

criteria.label: Effort interpretation
criteria.description: Treats difficulty as information, not a conclusion.

criteria.label: Meaningful chunk
criteria.description: Names a relationship that organizes the material.

content.prompt: A learner rereads a four-step explanation until it feels easy, then cannot explain step three an hour later. What is the next practice move?
content.solution: Do not let ease count as proof. Ask for the explanation from memory, find the missing link, reorganise the steps by why each one follows, and check again later.

content.title: Use the help, then pull it away
content.body: First explain each labelled step in a worked example. Next solve a similar case with the labels gone. Finally sort any error into a type and change one condition for the retry.

criteria.label: Faded support
criteria.description: Moves from an example to a less-supported attempt.

criteria.label: Error-informed retry
criteria.description: Classifies an error and changes the retry.

content.prompt: You have just watched a worked example of a problem type you have never tried. Design your next three attempts.
content.solution: Attempt one annotates why each step works. Attempt two strips the annotations out. Attempt three uses the error feedback to pick a changed but similar problem.

content.title: Run your own experiment
content.body: The scaffolding is gone. State a target, a practice condition, a later marker, and the single change you will make if that marker comes back weak.

criteria.label: Inspectable plan
criteria.description: Names target, condition, and later check.

criteria.label: Evidence-based reflection
criteria.description: Compares a record with a prediction.

content.title: Your one-week learning experiment
content.brief: Pick a small target. Plan two practice attempts and a delayed marker, record what actually happened, then rewrite next week’s condition from what you found.
content.deliverable: A short plan, a record of the result, and one revision backed by evidence.
rubric: The plan names a target and the later evidence.
The reflection cites a record, not just a feeling.
The adaptation is specific enough to test.

references.citation: Koedinger, K. R., Corbett, A. T., & Perfetti, C. (2012). The Knowledge-Learning-Instruction framework: Bridging the science-practice chasm to enhance robust student learning.

modules.title: What proves you’ve actually learned it?
How do you get it back when you need it?
What is the struggle actually telling you?
What kind of help actually helps?
